entries.name: Best-first search
entries.persistent_id: Linear-Space Best-First Search: Summary of Results
entries.definition: A search strategy that repeatedly expands the open node with the best value under a specified evaluation rule, adding eligible successors to the open frontier.
entries.identity_notes: This record describes the canonical global minimum-f form, with lower values defined as better. A-star, heuristic-only greedy best-first search and weighted A-star choose different evaluation rules. Broader literature also calls restricted-candidate-set policies best-first; their extra selection rules are not part of this core procedure. BFS is not an alias here because it identifies breadth-first search in AIMech.

source.title: Linear-Space Best-First Search: Summary of Results

entries.locator: Introduction, printed p. 533 / PDF p. 1: open/closed lists, minimum-f expansion and special cases
entries.mechanism: Maintain an open frontier of generated nodes eligible for expansion. Select a node with minimum evaluation value, test the selected node for a goal, and otherwise expand it and update the frontier under the chosen duplicate policy. The evaluation rule and duplicate handling determine the specific search algorithm.
limitations: A minimum evaluation value alone does not guarantee minimum solution cost; the meaning and assumptions of the evaluation rule matter.
Maintaining the full frontier and explored-state information can require substantial memory. Recursive or bounded-memory variants change what is retained.
Tie-breaking, duplicate updates and termination conditions are additional algorithm choices; the generic strategy does not settle them or guarantee completion on an infinite space.

entries.name: Greedy best-first search
entries.definition: A best-first search algorithm that prioritizes open nodes by a heuristic estimate of remaining cost to a goal, without adding the cost already incurred to that priority.
entries.identity_notes: The identity is heuristic-only global best-first selection, not every algorithm described as greedy. Hill climbing and beam search restrict the available candidates differently. The accumulated cost may still be stored for reconstructing or measuring a solution; it is omitted from the primary priority key.

source.title: A Comparison of Greedy Search Algorithms
source.version: SoCS 1(1), 129–136 (2010); author-hosted manuscript with unnumbered PDF pages

entries.locator: Best-First Search: Greedy best-first search and Ignoring Duplicates, PDF p. 2; family distinctions on PDF p. 1
entries.mechanism: Select a node with minimum heuristic value h from the open frontier, expand it, and place eligible successors on that frontier until a selected goal or another stopping condition is reached. The cost-to-date g does not contribute to this heuristic-only primary ranking.
limitations: The priority rule supplies no user-chosen fixed bound on solution suboptimality. Any post-hoc bound requires additional lower-bound information and assumptions.
Tie-breaking and duplicate handling remain consequential implementation choices. Completeness is not asserted for arbitrary infinite spaces or memory-pruned variants.
A strong cost-to-go heuristic does not by itself establish universally fast search; no empirical correlation threshold is treated as a general theorem.

entries.name: Weighted A-star search
entries.definition: A heuristic best-first search algorithm that orders open nodes by g+w h using a fixed finite weight w greater than one, where g is path cost so far and h estimates remaining cost.
entries.identity_notes: The record concerns fixed-weight Weighted A-star, not a depth-dependent weight schedule, an anytime schedule of repeated searches, or weighted IDA-star. Pohl’s original expression (1−omega)g+omega h uses a different parameterization; for omega less than one, dividing by the positive factor (1−omega) gives w=omega/(1−omega), so w>1 corresponds to omega>1/2. This algebraic equivalence concerns priority ordering, not duplicate-policy equivalence.

source.title: When Does Weighted A* Fail?

entries.locator: Introduction, PDF p. 1: f-prime(n)=g(n)+w h(n), w in (1,infinity)
entries.mechanism: Maintain a best-first frontier ranked by the cost already incurred plus a fixed amplified heuristic estimate, g+w h. The weight changes the tradeoff in node ordering while graph duplicate handling, tie-breaking and stopping rules must still be specified.
limitations: Increasing the weight does not guarantee faster search or fewer expansions. The cited study’s empirical conditions are not asserted as necessary-and-sufficient conditions on all search spaces.

A w-suboptimality guarantee requires an admissible heuristic and appropriate graph-search and termination conditions. It must not be inferred from the priority formula alone or an implementation that indiscriminately drops improved duplicates.
The weight is finite and fixed in this record; w=1 gives the A-star priority, while a heuristic-only priority is curated separately.

entries.name: Simple recursive best-first search
entries.persistent_id: Linear-Space Best-First Search: Summary of Results
entries.definition: A recursive best-first search procedure that initializes generated children from their static evaluation values, explores the best child within an alternative-derived bound, and backs up returned values to decide which subtree to revisit.
entries.identity_notes: SRBFS is Korf’s simple recursive algorithm, not an alias for the full RBFS refinement. It resets regenerated children to their static values instead of conditionally inheriting a previously backed-up parent value. This distinction can cause additional regeneration.

source.title: Linear-Space Best-First Search: Summary of Results

entries.locator: Simple Recursive Best-First Search, printed pp. 534–535 / PDF pp. 2–3; SRBFS pseudocode and Figure 3
entries.mechanism: Initialize each child’s stored value from its static evaluation and keep the children ordered by those values. Recurse into the best child with the smaller of the current bound and the next-best sibling’s value, then replace that child’s stored value with the returned value and reorder. Backtrack when the best available child exceeds the bound; a dead end returns infinity.
limitations: Resetting regenerated child values can repeat already explored work before reaching a previously established frontier. Full RBFS adds a conditional inheritance rule to mitigate this.
Path cycles and termination require appropriate graph and evaluation assumptions or explicit path checks; the displayed procedure is not a complete production implementation for every graph.
The recursive representation retains the path and sibling alternatives. Linear-in-depth memory is conditional on bounded branching and fixed-size node information; it is not full-frontier storage.

entries.name: Recursive best-first search
entries.persistent_id: Linear-Space Best-First Search: Summary of Results
entries.definition: A recursive search algorithm that explores the best stored subtree alternative within an upper bound and conditionally passes a previously backed-up value to regenerated children, retaining path and sibling information instead of the full best-first frontier.
entries.identity_notes: RBFS denotes Korf’s full refinement of SRBFS. A backed-up value greater than the node’s static value signals previous exploration; only then do child values inherit the maximum of that backed-up value and their own static evaluations. Unconditionally replacing every child value by the maximum with its parent’s value would lose this distinction for nonmonotone evaluation functions.

source.title: Linear-Space Best-First Search: Summary of Results

entries.locator: Full Recursive Best-First Search, printed p. 535 / PDF p. 3; Theoretical Results, printed p. 536 / PDF p. 4
entries.mechanism: For a node with static value f and stored value V, initialize each child from its static value unless V exceeds f, in which case use the maximum of V and the child’s static value. Recurse into the child with the smallest stored value using the smaller of the inherited bound and the next-best sibling value. Back up the returned value, reorder the children and switch subtrees when an alternative becomes preferable.
limitations: The paper’s best-first-order statement concerns newly expanded search-tree nodes. Previously expanded paths may be regenerated in depth-first order.
Path and sibling storage is O(bd) for branching factor b and maximum depth d under the paper’s model; linear-in-depth storage assumes bounded b and fixed-size node data.
Numerous distinct evaluation values can cause substantial regeneration overhead. The memory saving does not establish an A-star-equivalent runtime bound.
If a cycle does not increase the evaluation value, explicit current-path cycle checking is needed to avoid looping; the method is not a global closed-list duplicate-elimination algorithm.

entries.name: Recursive best-first search with controlled re-expansion
entries.definition: An RBFS variant that estimates subtree evaluation-value distributions and inflates backed-up values to make later visits expand geometrically more nodes, while retaining original lower-bound information for solution-cost pruning.
entries.identity_notes: RBFS_CR is the histogram-based controlled re-expansion method of Hatem, Kiesel and Ruml. It is distinct from their fixed-tolerance RBFS-epsilon and weighted-root RBFS-kth-root heuristics. Its inflated ordering can depart from strict best-first order in the original evaluation values.

source.title: Recursive Best-First Search with Bounded Overhead
source.version: AAAI 29(1), 1151–1157 (2015); author-hosted manuscript with unnumbered PDF pages

entries.locator: RBFS with Controlled Re-expansion, Figure 2 and discussion, PDF pp. 3–4; Assumptions 1–3 and Theorem 2, PDF pp. 4–5
entries.mechanism: Maintain original backed-up values F and additional inflated values F_CR. Histograms of generated but pruned evaluation values guide the inflation so the next visit is estimated to perform geometrically more work. Use inflated values to control traversal and backtracking, and original bounds for branch-and-bound after an incumbent solution is available.
limitations: The published O(N) expansion analysis is conditional on accurate subtree histograms, enough counts to choose appropriate backups, and a bound of O(N) on extra unique nodes beyond optimal solution cost. N is the specified A-star search-tree expansion count without duplicate pruning and with worst-case ties.
The implementation’s finite histogram buckets estimate distributions; they do not automatically satisfy the analysis’s exact-distribution assumption on every problem.

The paper retains one histogram per current-path node. Its depth-linear storage argument assumes bounded per-node histogram and successor storage; an added unbounded transposition table changes the memory scope.

Liberal thresholds require continuing branch-and-bound after finding an incumbent to establish optimality under admissible bounds. The first encountered solution is not automatically certified optimal.
The record does not certify the pseudocode as a complete executable implementation or claim universal speed improvement.

source_caveats.observation: Text pp. 1–11 was inspected; rendered pp. 4,7,10 were visually read. The omega-to-w conversion is curator algebra about priority ordering, not an assertion that basic HPA duplicate handling equals modern Weighted A-star.

Core PDF pp. 1–4 were text/visually inspected. RBFS inherits backed-up values only when the parent’s stored value exceeds its static value. The memory expression retains branching factor; ordering new nodes is distinct from regeneration order.

Full method descriptions on PDF pp. 1–2 were read and p. 2 visually verified. The paper’s experimental duplicate-discard policy is not blanket evidence for a w-suboptimality guarantee. Remaining method families are leads.
Text PDF pp. 1–4,7–8 was read and p. 1 visually checked. The abstract’s iff correlation language summarizes empirical results; no universal characterization or benchmark number is imported.

All seven text pages were read; rendered pp. 2–6 were visually checked. The theorem uses exact-distribution, sufficient-count and extra-node assumptions. Practical bucketed estimates, relaxed original-f order, and an unlimited transposition table in one experiment are explicit limitations. The stored source is the paper, not the similarly named talk PDF.
